body: The DJ drops a cumbia at twenty to eleven and the floor fills in about four seconds. A man of twenty-six who has spent the whole reception at the bar end of the room is out there before he has decided to be, because his feet have known where the beat sits since before he could talk. His aunt is opposite him doing the thing with her shoulders. Somebody’s grandfather, who has not stood all evening, is up. Then the chorus arrives and the man does what he has done at every wedding since he was nine — mouths a shape that fits the syllables, loudly and confidently, without knowing what he is saying.
He is not pretending and he is not failing at anything. He is doing precisely what he has always done, which is to belong completely to the music and only partly to the words.
Latin Worship, sung in English. On paper it is the strangest entry on the whole band, and it prompts an obvious and reasonable question, which is who on earth it is supposed to be for.

It is for the second generation, and it is worth being exact about what that means, because the phrase gets used as though it described a stage on the way to somewhere. It does not. These are people raised in houses where the parents prayed in one language and the children answered in another, where the music at home was one thing and the music in the car park after school was another, and where both were native. Not one authentic and one adopted. Both. A person like this does not have a first language and a second language so much as two incomplete ones, each carrying a different half of their life, and no amount of practice will merge them, because they were never separate enough to merge.

The dial runs from HM 300.30 to HM 398.70 and carries 121 stations. Familia Inspire holds HM 320.30 in Spanish for the global Spanish-speaking family, and is on air now. This other frequency is not its English translation, and that is the entire point.

It would have been far cheaper to build the translation. Take the Spanish station, commission English versions of the same songs, and you have a second frequency for the cost of a lyric sheet. What that produces is a station that no one is from. The reason this one costs more is that it keeps the musical inheritance whole — the ballad, the cumbia, the samba, the theatrical and liturgical shapes that make a song feel like a house you have been in before — and puts the listener’s actual thinking language on top of it. The second generation does not need a Spanish station or an English one. It needs the one that knows both are true at once.

Almost nothing in the culture is built this way, because identity is administered in boxes. A form asks for a language and permits one answer. A church runs a Spanish service at nine and an English service at eleven; the young people drift to the second and the grandparents hold the first, and nobody notices that this sorts one family into two congregations sharing a building. The music follows the same logic — playlists are filed by language because filing has to be done somehow. The person who is genuinely both gets classified as whichever half is easier to serve, and wonders why every station on offer feels like a slight misdescription of them.

On this dial that station is not filed with the international frequencies at all. It sits in the five-fold beat with the domestic stations, and its relays run from Miami, Los Angeles and San Antonio — the map of Latino life in the United States rather than the map of Latin America. Where a station puts its towers tells you who it thinks it is talking to, and this one is not broadcasting to a continent. It is broadcasting to a neighbourhood.
Which raises the objection that gets made every time, usually gently and usually by somebody older.

The objection is that a station like this accelerates a loss. If the grandchildren worship in English, the Spanish goes in a generation, and with it the prayers in the register they were first heard in, the specific words a grandmother used, and eventually the thing itself. That is a serious argument and it is not paranoid — languages have gone that way in every diaspora there has been, and quickly. But it mistakes where the loss happens. A language is not preserved by refusing to sing in the other one. It is preserved at home, on the phone on Sunday, in the insistence that a child answer their grandmother properly. What an English worship station decides is not whether Spanish survives, but whether a person who already thinks in English gets to worship in the language they think in.
Nobody has ever been formed by a song they had to translate first.

He is thirty-one and driving his daughter to school, and she asks from the back seat what a line in the song means. It is a song he has known his entire life. He starts to answer and finds he can give her the words — this one means river, this one means to lift up — and that the translation is correct and lands in the car as nothing at all. She says oh, and goes back to her tablet. He drives another mile and cannot let it go, because what the line means to him is his father in the front room on a Sunday afternoon with the windows open, and a particular smell, and being small. None of that was in the sentence he handed her.
He is not a bad translator. He is running into the thing translation cannot carry, which is everything a song picked up on the way to you.

There is a real cost to a station like this and it should be said plainly. It will not sound authentic to the generation above. To an ear formed in Bogotá or Guadalajara, worship in English over a cumbia will sound like a copy of something, and the judgement will be delivered kindly and will sting. It is also true that a listener who uses this frequency exclusively will find their Spanish getting worse rather than better, and the station will have played a part in that.

That discomfort is not a flaw in the format. It is what a genuinely in-between position feels like from either side, and the mistake would be to build a station that hides it. The alternative on offer is not a listener with two perfect languages. It is a listener who quietly stops singing, because both available stations require them to be somebody slightly other than they are, and the effort of the impersonation eventually exceeds the value of the worship. A frequency that is honest about the in-between is the only kind that person will keep.

So the strangest entry on the schedule turns out to be one of the plainest. It is a station for people whose musical formation and whose language of thought did not come from the same country, which is not a rare condition and is not a defect. It does not ask them to be more Latino at the door, or to leave the rhythm outside in exchange for being understood. It assumes both, plays both, and then gets on with the actual business, which is worship.
All of which is theory until something is actually playing. So here is the part that is not theory.

The dial carries four kinds of programming — music, which is most of it; teaching and prayer; family programming safe to have on in a room with children; and 40 international stations hosted across 29 languages for the nations rather than translated at them. There is one further frequency worth knowing about here: Inspire Latin holds HM 374.40, a family-safe Latin station for the whole household, and it is assigned and not yet on air.

Start at HM 310.90 — Latin Worship (English-Spanish), hosted by Santiago Inspire and carrying 482 tracks: Latin ballad, cumbia, samba and a theatrical, liturgical strand you will not hear anywhere else on the band. Its relays are Miami, Los Angeles and San Antonio, which is the tell. The catalogue is not a Spanish repertoire with English pasted over it and it is not an English repertoire with a percussion track added. It is what Santiago writes, which is Latin and South American worship for people who think in English, made for exactly the listener this article has been describing and not adapted towards them from either direction. Latin Worship Nights runs from seven in the evening.

There is nothing to install. No app, no download and no card — open kJubilee.com on whatever phone or laptop is nearest, press play, and it plays. It is deliberately built for inexpensive phones and thin connections, so it starts on the hardware people actually have. If you want it closer to hand, add the page to your home screen and it will open like anything else on it. And do make yourself an account while you are there. It keeps your favourites with you across every Jubilee site, and it is how this band learns which frequencies people are genuinely reaching for, which is how the next one gets built.

So take this as an invitation rather than an offer. Put HM 310.90 on this evening while you are cooking or driving, and pay attention to one thing only: whether you find yourself singing without first deciding to. That is the test that matters and it is not a matter of taste. It is the sound of the two halves briefly not being two halves, which is worth an evening of anybody’s time to find out about.
